outcomes.text: Explain the debate between conflict and consensus views of society.
Show how sociological ideas change over time and shape our view of the social world.
Outline the time, place and worldviews of Durkheim, Marx and Weber and what each contributed to sociology.
Compare feminist, functionalist, interactionist and Marxist views of social structures, processes and issues.
Read extracts from key texts and pick out the main arguments.
Link the core areas of sociology and apply research methods to families, education, crime and stratification.
Use key terms such as society, socialisation, norms, values, roles, labelling, discrimination, power and authority.

units.title: 3.2 Social structures, social processes and social issues

topics.title: 3.2 Social structures, social processes and social issues

outcomes.text: Critically evaluate and compare theories and explanations within each topic.
Respond to extracts showing sociologists' views and critically analyse how they interpret issues.
Understand methods issues such as official statistics, qualitative and quantitative data and mixed methods; debate contemporary social issues.
Identify and explain the sexual, reproductive, economic and educational functions of families.
Explain Parsons' functionalist view of primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities.
Compare functionalist, feminist and Marxist views on the functions of families.
Describe nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent and single sex families.
Compare how family forms differ in the UK and globally.
Explain the Rapoports' work on family diversity.
Describe and explain joint and segregated conjugal roles.
Explain the domestic division of labour in traditional and contemporary families.
Discuss decision making, money, dual career families, child rearing and leisure in couples.
Explain Oakley's feminist view of the conventional family and compare other perspectives.
Explain how family relationships changed from pre-industrial to industrial to modern times.
Discuss parenting quality, teenager-adult relations, care of disabled or elderly people and arranged marriage.
Describe Willmott and Young's symmetrical family and stratified diffusion; compare perspectives.
Explain criticisms of families such as isolation, idealisation, loss of functions, women's role and marital breakdown.
Compare functionalist, feminist and Marxist views of these criticisms.
Describe Zaretsky's Marxist view and Delphy and Leonard's feminist critique.
Describe the pattern of divorce in Britain since 1945 using statistics.
Explain reasons for rising divorce: law, attitudes, secularisation and women's status.
Describe divorce's effects on spouses, children, extended family and lone parent numbers.
Compare functionalist, feminist and Marxist views of divorce.
Explain how education serves the economy, social mobility and social cohesion.
Explain Durkheim's norms and values view and Parsons' achieved status and meritocracy.
Describe primary, secondary, state and private schools, and home schooling and de-schooling.
Compare functionalist, feminist and Marxist views of education's role.

topics.title: 3.4.2 The relationship between education and capitalism

outcomes.text: Describe Bowles and Gintis' correspondence principle linking education and capitalism.
Compare alternative views of the correspondence principle.
Explain how class, gender and ethnicity affect educational achievement.
Describe Halsey on class inequalities and Ball on parental choice and school competition.
Compare functionalist, feminist and Marxist views of achievement.
Explain streaming, setting, mixed ability teaching, labelling and the self-fulfilling prophecy.
Describe Ball on teacher expectations and Willis on counter school cultures.
Compare interactionist, functionalist, feminist and Marxist views of school processes.

topics.title: 3.5.1 The social construction of crime and deviance

outcomes.text: Explain the social construction of crime and deviance.
Explain anomie, labelling, structural, subcultural and interactionist theories of crime.
Describe Merton's functionalist and Becker's interactionist views of crime's causes.
Compare interactionist, functionalist, feminist and Marxist views.
Explain formal and informal social control, unwritten rules and sanctions.
Describe Heidensohn on female conformity in patriarchal societies.
Compare perspectives on social control.
Explain how class, gender, ethnicity and age affect criminal and deviant behaviour.
Describe Albert Cohen on delinquent subcultures and Carlen on women, crime and poverty.
Describe debates on violent crime, sentencing, young offenders, prisons and media coverage.
Compare perspectives on factors in criminal behaviour.
Describe the main sources of crime data and how official figures are collected.
Describe patterns and trends in crime figures using statistics.
Explain the dark figure: unreported and unrecorded crime.
Compare perspectives on using crime data.
Explain functionalist stratification: effective role allocation linked to rewards.
Describe Davis and Moore's key ideas and compare feminist and Marxist alternatives.
Explain socio-economic class divisions in society.
Describe Marx's and Weber's views of class and compare perspectives.
Explain how class, gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, age, disability and religion affect life chances.
Describe Devine's revisiting of the affluent worker and compare perspectives.
Explain interpretations of poverty: culture of poverty, material deprivation, government action, unemployment and globalisation.
Describe Townsend on relative deprivation and Murray on the underclass and the New Right.
Compare functionalist, feminist and Marxist views of poverty.
Explain traditional, charismatic and rational-legal authority and formal and informal power.
Describe Weber on power and authority and compare perspectives.
Explain how class, gender, sexuality, race, age, disability and religion shape power relationships.
Describe Walby on patriarchy and compare perspectives.
Explain research methods, their strengths and weaknesses for a given research area.
Explain research design, practical difficulties, ethical issues and primary and secondary sources.
Interpret data presented in different forms.
Explain aims, hypotheses, pilot studies, sampling methods and data analysis.
Explain questionnaires, interviews and observations and judge their value and limits.
Judge the usefulness of mixed methods.
Judge qualitative and quantitative data, official and non-official statistics, and primary and secondary sources.
Read graphs, charts, diagrams and tables to find patterns and trends.
Explain time, cost and access issues, and consent, confidentiality and harm, and how to address them.
